title: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)
subject: Medicine
summary: Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disease with skin thickening, vascular injury and organ fibrosis. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and serology; management focuses on organ protection and symptom control.

sections.p: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a chronic connective‑tissue disease characterised by immune activation, micro‑vascular injury and excessive collagen deposition. The 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria combine skin involvement, serology and internal organ disease to classify patients as limited or diffuse.
b: Limited cutaneous (CREST) – skin thickening distal to elbows/knees, calcinosis, Raynaud, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia
Diffuse cutaneous – widespread skin thickening, early visceral involvement

t.b: Positive ANA supports diagnosis; high titres of anti‑centromere suggest limited SSc, anti‑topoisomerase I (Scl‑70) suggest diffuse
Specific for limited cutaneous SSc; indicates lower risk of renal crisis but higher risk of pulmonary hypertension
Associated with diffuse SSc and interstitial lung disease
Detects pulmonary hypertension, pericardial effusion, LV dysfunction; normal in early disease but may evolve

sections.p: The modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS) quantifies skin thickness; a score >12 predicts poor survival. Organ‑specific scores (e.g., GAP for ILD) guide prognosis.
b: mRSS 0–5 – mild skin involvement
mRSS 6–12 – moderate
mRSS >12 – severe

sections.p: The exact trigger is unknown, but genetic susceptibility (HLA‑DRB1) and environmental exposures (silica, solvents) are implicated. In low‑resource settings, infections such as HIV and TB may coexist and worsen outcomes.
b: Genetic predisposition
Silica exposure
Infections (HIV, TB)

sections.p: Patients first notice Raynaud’s phenomenon, followed by skin tightening, digital ulcers and dysphagia. Early visceral signs include dyspnoea, cough, hypertension and proteinuria.
b: Raynaud’s attacks – cold‑induced pallor, cyanosis, pain
Digital ulcers – painful, slow healing
Esophageal dysmotility – regurgitation, heartburn

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the diagnosis, stage organ involvement and detect complications. In low‑resource settings, prioritize tests that are affordable and available.

t.b: Normal or mild changes in early disease; extensive fibrosis in advanced ILD
Normal in early disease; <70% predicted is concerning
Normal in early disease; rising creatinine indicates renal crisis
Normal in early disease; elevated PASP >35 mmHg is abnormal
Positive ANA in >90% of patients; specific antibodies guide prognosis

sections.p: Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) and pulmonary hypertension are life‑threatening. Early hypertension, sudden proteinuria or worsening dyspnoea warrant urgent review.
b: SRC – sudden rise in BP, oliguria, rising creatinine
Pulmonary hypertension – progressive dyspnoea, right heart failure
Digital gangrene – requires vascular assessment

sections.p: Treat the underlying autoimmune process, protect organs and relieve symptoms. In low‑resource settings, use generic immunosuppressants and supportive care.
b: Corticosteroids – short courses for severe flare
Cyclophosphamide – for diffuse ILD or renal crisis (if available)
Methotrexate – for skin disease
Antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors) – first line for SRC
Calcium channel blockers – Raynaud’s attacks

t.b: Avoid in pregnancy and with renal impairment

sections.p: Regular monitoring of skin score, lung function, blood pressure and renal parameters is essential. Vaccinations and infection prevention are critical in immunosuppressed patients.
b: Annual skin score assessment
Quarterly pulmonary function tests
Blood pressure monitoring twice daily in SRC
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza

sections.p: Other connective‑tissue diseases and vascular disorders can mimic SSc.
b: Systemic lupus erythematosus – similar skin rash but lacks sclerodactyly
Mixed connective tissue disease – overlap features but different serology
Vascular malformations – cause digital ulcers but no skin tightening

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal early in disease or affected by co‑morbidities.
b: ANA can be negative in early diffuse SSc
Pulmonary function may be normal until advanced ILD
Blood pressure may be masked by antihypertensives

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in blood pressure with oliguria
Severe unexplained pain or swelling of limbs

faq.q: What is the most specific antibody for limited cutaneous SSc?
faq.a: Anti‑centromere antibodies are highly specific for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

faq.q: Why are ACE inhibitors preferred in scleroderma renal crisis?
faq.a: They lower blood pressure and reduce intraglomerular pressure, slowing progression of renal failure.

faq.q: Can Raynaud’s phenomenon be the first sign of systemic sclerosis?
faq.a: Yes, Raynaud’s attacks often precede other manifestations by months or years.

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with Raynaud’s attacks and sclerodactyly. Which antibody is most likely positive? — Anti‑centromere; indicates limited cutaneous disease and lower risk of renal crisis.
A patient with diffuse SSc develops sudden hypertension and oliguria. What is the immediate management? — Start an ACE inhibitor; consider plasma exchange if renal failure progresses.

During a ward round, you notice a patient with scleroderma has a new onset dyspnoea. Which investigation should you order first? — Pulmonary function tests (spirometry and DLCO) to assess for interstitial lung disease.
A scleroderma patient develops digital ulcers. Which drug is least likely to help? — Prednisone; it may worsen ulcer healing compared to calcium channel blockers.
A patient with CREST syndrome complains of dysphagia. What is the most likely pathophysiology? — Esophageal dysmotility due to smooth‑muscle fibrosis.
In a low‑resource setting, which test is essential to confirm systemic sclerosis if serology is unavailable? — Clinical criteria: skin thickening distal to elbows/knees plus Raynaud’s attacks.
